question: Distinguish a codified constitution from an uncodified one; describe two ways constitutional monarchs can differ in power.

draft.raw:

claims.subject: codified constitution
claims.text: A codified constitution is a constitution that is written down into a single document or set of legal documents, whereas an uncodified constitution is not encompassed in a single comprehensive document and is instead composed of multiple sources such as fundamental acts, court cases, and treaties.

references.label: P1.1
references.text: A constitution, or supreme law, is the aggregate of fundamental principles or established precedents that constitute the legal basis of a polity, organization or other type of entity, and commonly determines how that entity is to be governed.[1]

references.label: P2.1
references.text: When these principles are written down into a single document or set of legal documents, those documents may be said to embody a written constitution; if they are encompassed in a single comprehensive document, it is said to embody a codified constitution.

references.label: P2.2
references.text: The constitution of the United Kingdom is a notable example of an uncodified constitution; it is instead written in numerous fundamental acts of a legislature, court cases, and treaties.[2]

claims.subject: constitutional monarch
claims.text: Constitutional monarchs can differ in power in that some have virtually no executive or policy-making power and are primarily symbolic heads of state, while others have meaningful formal powers such as veto power, appointment power, and the power to dissolve parliament.

references.label: P5.1
references.text: The powers of constitutional monarchs vary.

references.label: P5.2
references.text: In some countries, the monarch has virtually no executive or policy-making power and is primarily a hereditary symbolic head of state (who may be an emperor, king or queen, prince or grand duke),[6] while in other countries, the monarch has meaningful formal powers (such as veto power, appointment power, and power to dissolve parliament).[7][8]

rendered:
A codified constitution is a constitution that is written down into a single document or set of legal documents, whereas an uncodified constitution is not encompassed in a single comprehensive document and is instead composed of multiple sources such as fundamental acts, court cases, and treaties. [1]
Constitutional monarchs can differ in power in that some have virtually no executive or policy-making power and are primarily symbolic heads of state, while others have meaningful formal powers such as veto power, appointment power, and the power to dissolve parliament. [2]
